opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started as something we built for ourselves. We kept running into the same wall: we'd have a model doing something interesting, and we'd have no good way to see *why*. We'd poke at it with ad hoc scripts, notebooks scattered everywhere, half-remembered experiments. So Silico began as internal tooling, a way to make that investigative loop faster and less painful for our own team.

The turning point was realizing how many other people were stuck in the same place. Every time we talked with researchers at other labs, or engineers at companies deploying models in production, we'd describe what we were doing and they'd say, "Wait, can I use that?" It wasn't just interpretability specialists either. It was people who needed to debug a model's behavior, understand a failure, or build enough confidence to ship something. The demand was coming from well beyond the research community.

There was also a bigger conviction underneath it. If understanding what's happening inside these systems only happens inside a handful of frontier labs, that's a fragile situation for everyone. Models are getting more capable and more widely deployed, and the ability to inspect and steer them shouldn't be a luxury. Making Silico available to others felt like a way to widen the circle of people who can actually look under the hood, and frankly, to learn much faster ourselves. When more people use a tool on more problems, you find out very quickly what's useful and what's just a nice demo.

So it was a mix of pull from users and a belief that this kind of capability needs to be broadly accessible. Once both of those were clearly true, keeping it internal didn't make much sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started as an internal tool. We'd built Silico for ourselves because we were drowning in the same problem every team working with these models hits: you make a change, you think it's better, and you have no real way to know. Running real experiments was slow, expensive, and often you'd get the signal weeks after you'd already moved on. So we built a way to simulate the outcome first, to run the experiment in silico before running it in vivo, and it just quietly became the thing we checked before shipping anything.

The moment it clicked was when we started talking to other companies and realized they were all building some janky version of the same thing. Spreadsheets, hand-rolled eval scripts, a prompt somebody wrote at 2 a.m. that everyone was afraid to touch. Everyone had the problem, nobody had solved it well, and most of them didn't want to be in the business of solving it. They wanted to build their product.

And then there was a more selfish reason. The simulations only get good when you have a lot of ground truth to calibrate against. One company's data is a trickle. If Silico lived inside many organizations, each running real experiments and feeding back what actually happened, the predictions get better for everyone. That flywheel doesn't exist if it stays an internal tool. So it was partly conviction that the problem was general, and partly recognizing that the thing we wanted most, accurate simulation, was only achievable at scale.

Once we started thinking about it in that second way, the product opportunity became much clearer. Could we take something useful to us and make it useful to someone who didn’t have our context or technical background? That was the motivation for making Silico available to others.

sol-6.1.text:
The turning point was realizing that what we were building for ourselves could be useful to other people, too. With Silico, you could take an idea, put it in front of simulated people, and explore how they might respond. That made it possible to ask questions that would otherwise be expensive or slow to investigate.

I don’t think the value is that a simulation gives you a definitive answer. It’s that it helps you sharpen your thinking: what assumptions are you making, what reactions haven’t you considered, and what should you go test with real people? Once we started thinking about it that way, it felt like something worth making available beyond our own team.

r001.rationale: The response says Silico could help others explore how simulated people might respond and sharpen assumptions; it does not identify agents accelerating the team’s own AI research as the reason.
